prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, opening moire quantum matter.

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the case in which a concrete theoretical prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald's continuum-model flat bands at a magic angle) was followed by an experimental surprise that nobody had asked for: correlated insulators and superconductivity in a carbon-only system, observed by Jarillo-Herrero's group. That sequence of prediction, then nature answering more richly than expected, is what I look for in a discovery. It also created a whole platform, with tunable twist angle, gating and many follow-on moire systems. The colleagues' openings show it is the only candidate ranked by all eight members and in the top three or so by five of them, which I treat as a sign of breadth of respect rather than as merit in itself. The theory-plus-experiment triple is coherent within the supplied names.
statement.case_against: The field is young. The pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated states are still debated, and sample and twist-angle disorder make comparison between groups difficult. A prize now could look early compared with B055 or B015, which have longer track records of settled interpretation. The credited names also leave out other experimental and theoretical contributors, so the attribution is not clean.

responses.point: Ranks the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp topological insulator candidate (B055) first because it is conceptually clean, thoroughly confirmed over fifteen years and has had lasting influence on materials theory, with B006 second and arguably a little early.
responses.response: I agree that B055 is the more settled case and I ranked it second myself. Where I differ is on the weight of attribution: the Z2 and quantum spin Hall story has contested priority among Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu, who are outside the supplied names, and any three-person prize would leave some of the central theorists out. B006 has a cleaner division of labour between the prediction and the decisive experiment. I accept that the superconducting mechanism is unresolved, but the discovery of the phases does not depend on the mechanism, so I would not call the prize premature. B055 stays my first alternative, and I could move to it if the committee judges maturity to outweigh novelty.

responses.point: Puts optical lattice clocks (B015) first as a clear, original, field-defining advance in precision measurement, with Katori and Ye as a clean two-person pair and confirmation across many laboratories.
responses.response: The attribution for B015 is the cleanest on the table and I take the maturity argument seriously. My reservation is about the type of discovery. The clock is a superb instrument and an enabling invention, but the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 prizes already cover neighbouring metrology, and the discovery-of-nature element, such as a new relativistic or fundamental-constant result, is still prospective. I would want the committee to say what the lattice clock has taught us about nature, rather than how precisely it measures. Your question of whether the redefinition of the second should come first seems to me a fair test I cannot settle from the evidence supplied. I keep B015 as my second alternative rather than my first choice.

responses.point: Ranks the IceCube high-energy neutrino discovery (B007) first as a decisive instrument-plus-discovery case, with a confirmed diffuse flux and the TXS 0506+056 and Galactic-plane results, while admitting that splitting credit within the collaboration is uncertain.
responses.response: I share your enthusiasm for B007 as a genuine new window on the cosmos and I placed it third. I disagree that the maturity is as strong as you suggest. The flux is established, but the sources and production mechanisms are still only partly identified, and an award citing the opening of neutrino astronomy sits uneasily with an astrophysical interpretation that is incomplete. The allocation among Halzen, Karle and Spiering, with AMANDA and Baikal predecessors outside the credit, is also hard to defend in a collaboration of this size. I would not block it, but I do not think it is ready to beat a candidate with a clearer individual allocation.

responses.point: Treats B015 as original and mature, resting on atomic-structure ideas such as magic wavelengths, and notes that the 2025 prize and possible overlaps affect B024 and the framing of clock candidates.
responses.response: Your point that the magic-wavelength idea is conceptually elegant and rests on real atomic-structure insight is well taken, and it strengthens B015 for me. I was less convinced that it should rank above B006, because the closer comparison is on how much new physics each opened. Your remark that the clock prize must be framed as distinct from the comb and ion work is the key requirement, and a short citation naming the magic-wavelength lattice would need to make that distinction. I do not see a reason to deny B015 a place in a final configuration; it is the cleanest two-person option if the committee prefers settled maturity.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards moire quantum matter as mature enough, given the unresolved pairing mechanism and sample dependence.
Credit for other early twisted-graphene theory and for experimental groups with parallel results is outside the supplied names, and I have not independently verified priority details.
Whether B055 or B015 should displace B006 if maturity and clean attribution carry more weight than novelty.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My professional connections are David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, none of whom are credited names on the shortlist as far as I can tell.
